papers.title: A Survey on Transfer Learning for Low-Resource Language Technologies: A Focused Survey of Transformer-Based Code-Mixed Language Identification and Zero-Shot Multilingual Speech Synthesis
papers.abstract: Most progress in natural language and speech processing has been achieved for a small group of languages with abundant labelled data, while languages with limited corpora and tooling continue to be underserved. This survey examines how transfer learning is used to narrow that gap in two complementary settings: word-level language identification of romanized Malayalam–English code-mixed social media text, and zero-shot multilingual multi-speaker text-to-speech synthesis for Indonesian, Javanese, and Sundanese. Two peer-reviewed studies are analysed in depth and placed in context using the literature they cite. A taxonomy of transfer strategies is proposed that distinguishes data-centric corpus construction, full finetuning of pretrained transformer encoders, shape-matched and partial parameter transfer, frozen pretrained modules used as feature extractors or perceptual critics, and explicit conditioning on language, speaker, and style. The historical development of word-level language identification and of speaker adaptation in neural speech synthesis is traced, and the evaluation practices of both lines of work are compared. The analysis shows that both studies report large gains over their in-study baselines, but that these gains depend on heuristically labelled or pooled small datasets, single evaluation splits, and, in the speech case, an objective metric that shares its encoder with the training loss. Open problems include reliable gold-standard annotation, class imbalance, orthographic variation, decoupled evaluation, and responsible use of voice cloning. Research directions such as code-mixed speech synthesis driven by token-level language tags are outlined

reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech synthesis, text-to-speech, voice cloning

papers.title: DESKXI: Design and Development of a Voice-First Desktop AI Mentor for Interactive Learning, Personalized Study Assistance, and Intelligent Task Management
papers.abstract: Students who study alone rarely have a tutor, an interview coach and a study planner within reach, and screen-based assistants pull attention away from the work itself. DESKXI is a voice-first desktop AI mentor that combines these roles in one device: it teaches by conversation, runs mock interviews, sets spoken quizzes, keeps Pomodoro study cycles, delivers reminders and retains durable facts about the learner between sessions, all through a streaming cloud speech-to-speech model. This paper describes how DESKXI divides work between the cloud model, which carries the open-ended conversation, and deterministic local services, which hold exact state such as timers, reminders and quiz keys. It also describes the real-time client runtime that carries these functions: a bounded drop-oldest capture queue, a writer-thread playback path, a microphone mute gate, a threetier recovery design and a SQLite store. We examine selected parts of this runtime by running the unmodified source code on a reference workstation with only the hardware and cloud modules stubbed. The measurements identified four limitations that matter for mentoring: speech that keeps playing for about 1.1 s after the learner interrupts, an unfiltered down-sampler that folds out-of-band energy into the speech band, reminders that fire up to 0.95 s early, and a quiz-answer parser that reached 44.6 % accuracy on our author-written stress set. We give a remedy for each. Learning outcomes were not studied
papers.venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: speech-to-speech

papers.title: What Makes a Good Audio Prompt for Zero-Shot TTS? Learning Prompt Selection from Synthesis Outcomes
papers.abstract: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) models clone a target voice from a short reference clip, commonly referred to as the prompt. In practice, the prompt has to be cut from a longer recording of the speaker, so which part to use must be chosen. To understand what makes a good prompt, we analyze hundreds of thousands of outputs synthesized by four TTS models from candidate prompts of YouTube recordings. The choice of prompt substantially changes intelligibility, naturalness and speaker similarity. Standard predicted-quality scores capture mainly the naturalness part but miss most of the intelligibility gain. We find that the models largely agree on which prompt yields the highest measured speaker similarity, but much less on which prompt yields intelligible speech. We propose a small network that learns from the outputs a TTS model produced to rank a recording's candidate prompts from their audio alone. Without synthesizing anything at selection time, it picks prompts that lower the word error rate on held-out recordings by a third (Qwen3-TTS) to two fifths (F5-TTS) relative to a randomly chosen prompt, more than predicted quality achieves and nearly as much as synthesizing a dozen test sentences from every candidate first.

papers.title: EmpDPO: Enabling Emphasis Control in TTS via Direct Preference Optimization
papers.abstract: Word-level emphasis conveys meaning that text alone cannot express and is therefore essential for a practical text-to-speech (TTS) system. In this work, we study how to add emphasis control post hoc to a pretrained TTS model that has never been trained with emphasis annotations. We present EmpDPO, a simple, efficient, and effective two-stage recipe that adds emphasis control to a multilingual zero-shot diffusion TTS model through supervised fine-tuning followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). The training signals for both stages come from an off-the-shelf multilingual emphasis detector, so that no manual emphasis annotation or task-specific reward design is needed. We find that DPO can substantially strengthen emphasis control with only a few thousand preference pairs and training steps. Objective and subjective evaluations against strong public systems show that our model produces perceptible emphasis while preserving naturalness and overall quality.
papers.venue: 5 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to ICASSP 2027. Audio samples: https://chaonan99.github.io/empdpo-demo/

# YuE2 B70 Turbo

Real-time AI music generation on one **Intel Arc Pro B70**. This repo is a recipe, not new weights: it runs the
unmodified [YuE2 3B](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-3B) GGUF from
[audio-cpp/Yue2-3B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/audio-cpp/Yue2-3B-GGUF) through
[audio.cpp](https://github.com/JarodMica/audio.cpp) on SYCL, with three small ggml-sycl fixes and one setting change.

**Result:** with guidance at 1.0, songs up to about **4:45** render faster than they play. A 4:20 song renders in
4:09 (1.04x real time). Stock settings render the same song in 6:54 (0.63x).

![Every song rendered on one Arc Pro B70: render time against song length](charts/renders.png)

![One 4:20 song, two recipes: where the render time goes](charts/recipe.png)

Every point is a solo render: one job on the B70 at a time. Nine early renders had shared the GPU with another job, which
slowed them up to 5x; each was re-rendered alone with the same settings and only the solo run is counted. All runs:
[`results/all-renders.csv`](results/all-renders.csv). The 42 finished songs and their render times are below.

## Real-time sweep

Measured 2026-10-29 on the Turbo box (Intel Arc Pro B70, oneAPI 2026.1, Level Zero). YuE2 3B q8_0, f16 VAE,
`cot=off`, 8 NAR steps, one render at a time. Raw numbers: [`results/realtime-sweep.csv`](results/realtime-sweep.csv).

| song length | render time | x real time | semantic (AR) | NAR | VAE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1:36 | 56 s | 1.71 | 34 s | 18 s | 3 s |
| 2:30 | 108 s | 1.39 | 65 s | 37 s | 5 s |
| 3:20 | 169 s | 1.19 | 99 s | 62 s | 7 s |
| 4:20 | 249 s | 1.04 | 140 s | 100 s | 9 s |
| 4:50 | 295 s | 0.98 | 162 s | 122 s | 10 s |
| 5:10 | 327 s | 0.95 | 178 s | 138 s | 10 s |
| 4:20, guidance 1.01 (stock) | 414 s | 0.63 | 306 s | 98 s | 9 s |

The NAR stage grows faster than song length because it runs as one chunk over the whole song, so it is the next lever.

## What changed

1. **Three ggml-sycl ops** YuE2 needs that audio.cpp's SYCL backend lacked ([`patches/0001-ggml-sycl-yue2-ops.patch`](patches/0001-ggml-sycl-yue2-ops.patch)):
   - `ROUND_BF16`: a unary op that exists only in audio.cpp's ggml fork. New SYCL kernel using the same
     round-to-nearest-even and quiet-NaN rule as `ggml_compute_fp32_to_bf16`, f32/f16/bf16 in, f32 out.
   - `EXPM1`: ported from upstream llama.cpp's ggml-sycl (used by SELU in YuE2's NAR).
   - `concat` for F16/BF16: ported from upstream llama.cpp's ggml-sycl (was F32/I32 only).
   - The unsupported-op error now names the unary op, which is how the first two were found.
2. **`guidance_scale=1.0`.** The default 1.01 runs classifier-free guidance, two sequences per token. At exactly 1.0
   YuE2 takes its single-sequence path, which makes the semantic stage about 2.2x faster.

## Reproduce

```bash
git clone https://github.com/JarodMica/audio.cpp && cd audio.cpp   # tested at 4dbb4d1
patch -p1 < 0001-ggml-sycl-yue2-ops.patch
source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh
cmake -S . -B build/sycl-yue2 -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=icx -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=icpx -DGGML_SYCL=ON -DGGML_SYCL_TARGET=INTEL -DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON \
  -DAUDIOCPP_MODEL_SET=custom -DAUDIOCPP_MODELS=yue2
ninja -C build/sycl-yue2 audiocpp_cli
hf download audio-cpp/Yue2-3B-GGUF yue2-3b-q8_0.gguf yue2-vae-f16.gguf sidecars/yue2-model-config.json \
  sidecars/yue2-generation-config.json sidecars/yue2-qwen.tiktoken sidecars/yue2-vae-config.json --local-dir models/Yue2-3B-GGUF

ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=level_zero:gpu build/sycl-yue2/bin/audiocpp_cli --task gen --family yue2 \
  --model models/Yue2-3B-GGUF --backend sycl --threads 8 \
  --lyrics "$(cat songs/'Trap Sessions'/'Moonwell Lean (seed 4242).txt')" \
  --request-option style="slow psychedelic R&B trap, dreamy, harp, celesta, ethereal female rap vocal" \
  --request-option cot=off --request-option guidance_scale=1.0 --seed 4242 --out song.wav
```

[`scripts/`](scripts/) has the sweep (`sweep-realtime.sh`), the batch renderer (`render-batch.sh`), and the
post-processing tools that trim dead tails and encode MP3 (`finish_track.py`, `wav2mp3.py`, `resample.py`, which
need numpy and PyAV). Point them at your build and model:

```bash
export AUDIOCPP_CLI=$PWD/build/sycl-yue2/bin/audiocpp_cli YUE2_MODEL=$PWD/models/Yue2-3B-GGUF
scripts/sweep-realtime.sh songs/'Trap Sessions'/'Moonwell Lean (seed 4242).txt' 2400 3750 5000 6500   # 1:36, 2:30, 3:20, 4:20
scripts/render-batch.sh my-songs/      # my-songs/manifest.json: [{"slug", "title", "style", "seed"}], lyrics in <slug>.txt
```
Notes from running it:
- Generation is not deterministic run to run on SYCL. Pass `export_semantic=true` and keep the token file if you may
  want to extend a take later with `semantic_prefix_file`.
- Sustained renders hold the B70 near 230 W and 82-83 C.

Âm thanh được tạo ra và phát ngay lập tức, " "không cần chờ toàn bộ đoạn văn hoàn thành. Nhờ vậy, người nghe chỉ mất " "khoảng 70 mili giây là đã nghe thấy câu đầu tiên, ngay cả khi mô " "hình đang chạy trên CPU của một chiếc laptop bình thường.") pending, tail = queue.Queue(), np.zeros(0, dtype="float32") def feed(outdata, frames, _time, _status): global tail while len(tail) < frames and not pending.empty(): tail = np.concatenate([tail, pending.get_nowait()]) n = min(frames, len(tail)) outdata[:n, 0] = tail[:n] outdata[n:] = 0 tail = tail[n:] with sd.OutputStream(samplerate=tts.sample_rate, channels=1, dtype="float32", callback=feed): for chunk in tts.synthesize_stream(TEXT, voice="maichi"): pending.put(chunk.reshape(-1)) # chunk is (1, n) float32 at 48 kHz while not pending.empty() or len(tail): sd.sleep(50) # let the buffer drain before closing ``` ## Benchmarks Measured on **[ZeroBench-TTS](https://huggingface.co/datasets/zeroweight-ai/ZeroBench-TTS)** Every system reads **raw text** — dates, numbers and acronyms verbatim, exactly as they appear in the wild, with no text frontend in front of the model. | | **ZeroTTS** | OmniVoice | XTTS-v2-vietnamse | viXTTS | |---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:| | **WER** ↓ | **1.03 %** | 4.13 % | 16.42 % | 18.40 % | | **Naturalness** (UTMOS) ↑ | **2.91** | 2.76 | 2.43 | 2.35 | | **Voice similarity** (SSIM) ↑ | 0.936 | **0.950** | 0.940 | 0.935 | | **Dead air** (excess silence) ↓ | **0.029 s** | 0.340 s | 0.532 s | 0.233 s | | **RTF, CPU** ↓ | **0.50×** | 6.12× | 0.71× | 0.73× | | **Time to first audio, CPU** ↓ | **~70 ms** | ~34 s | ~6.1 s | ~5.1 s | | **Parameters** ↓ | **202 M** | 775 M | 467 M | 467 M | **4× fewer word errors than the next-best system**, and the fastest of the four on CPU. The gap is much wider in latency than in throughput: the two XTTS fine-tunes also beat real time (0.71×) but need seconds to emit their first sample, while OmniVoice is 6× *slower* than real time. All three are sized and tuned for a GPU, and it shows. Full comparison tables, per-subset breakdowns, and CPU speed methodology: **[docs/BENCHMARKS.md](https://github.com/zeroweight-ai/ZeroTTS/blob/main/docs/BENCHMARKS.md)** ### Speed — CPU RTF (realtime factor, wall-clock synthesis time ÷ output audio duration — lower is faster; below 1× is faster than real time) and time-to-first-audio, all measured **on CPU**, single request, 8 inference threads pinned to a dedicated core pool (no other synthesis running concurrently). Three Vietnamese samples — short (26 chars), medium (77 chars), long (227 chars) — each run 6 times with the first 2 (cold-cache) discarded; figures below are the mean of the remaining 4. | | **ZeroTTS** | OmniVoice | XTTS-v2-vietnamse | viXTTS | |---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:| | RTF — short | **0.51×** | 10.87× | 0.70× | 0.71× | | RTF — medium | **0.47×** | 4.82× | 0.70× | 0.70× | | RTF — long | **0.53×** | 2.67× | 0.71× | 0.78× | | TTFA — short | **53 ms** | 21.7 s | 4.02 s | 2.45 s | | TTFA — medium | **66 ms** | 28.9 s | 4.02 s | 3.72 s | | TTFA — long | **89 ms** | 52.3 s | 10.3 s | 9.22 s | ZeroTTS's time-to-first-audio comes from its real streaming path — first audio frame, not first full utterance. The three baselines have no working CPU streaming path, so their TTFA is the time to the complete utterance. ## Voices, and voice cloning A voice is a small array of speaker latents, `(1, n_voice_queries, d_model)`, shipped as a `.npz` under `voices/`. That array is the entire speaker conditioning — no reference transcript, no audio prompt. > **Voice cloning is not available in this release.** Those latents come from a > voice encoder that reads a reference clip, and that encoder is not published. > This repository ships ready-to-use voices; it cannot create new ones from > audio. > > To get latents for your own speaker, see **[zeroweight.ai](https://zeroweight.ai)** > or get in touch. Because a voice is just an array, latents obtained that way drop into `voices//voice.npz` and work with no code change. ## Intended use and limitations Built for **Vietnamese**. It handles English words embedded in Vietnamese text (`code_switch`), but it is not an English TTS system and is not evaluated as one. Do not use it to impersonate a real person, to generate speech attributed to someone without their consent, or to produce audio intended to deceive. The shipped voices are for evaluation and demos. Synthetic speech should be disclosed as synthetic wherever a listener might reasonably assume otherwise. ## Credits Speech codec: **MOSS-Audio-Tokenizer-Nano** by the OpenMOSS team, Apache-2.0. The ZeroBench-TTS *dataset* is CC-BY-NC-4.0 because it redistributes reference audio from VIVOS, viVoice, phoaudiobook and Emilia. That license applies to the benchmark dataset only — **not** to these weights.

# KittenTTS 2

A 1.7B speech language model with in-context voice cloning. It reads text and writes S3
codec tokens, which a vocoder turns into 24 kHz audio.

```bash
pip install kittenml
```

```python
from kittenml import KittenTTS
import soundfile as sf

m = KittenTTS("KittenML/kitten-tts-2")

# a built-in voice
audio = m.generate("Hi! umm.. how are you, I guess?  .. uh.. nice to meet you??",
                   voice="WeatherPresenterCheerful")

# or clone one, from 5-30 seconds of a single speaker
audio = m.generate("This is my own voice.", reference="my_voice.wav")

sf.write("output.wav", audio, m.sample_rate)
```

Everything the model needs is in this repository, so no Hugging Face login is required.

## Voices

`m.available_voices` lists all 115. Bella, Jasper, Luna, Bruno, Rosie, Hugo, Kiki
and Leo are the same speakers as in KittenTTS 0.8, so existing code keeps working.

Voices named after a person are English. The rest are named for the language they
speak followed by what they are — `SpanishAbuela`, `JapaneseTrainConductor`,
`RussianBabushka` — and are how you reach those languages, since the voice is what
carries the accent. Nine older entries carry a bare language name: Arabic, Chinese,
French, German, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish.

```python
m.generate("Guten Morgen. Ich wünsche dir einen wunderschönen Tag.",
           voice="German", normalize=False)

m.generate("Buenas tardes. Hoy vamos a preparar algo muy especial.",
           voice="SpanishAbuela", normalize=False)
```

Sixteen languages have a named voice: Arabic, Chinese, Dutch, French, German, Hindi,
Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Turkish,
and English.

Pass `normalize=False` for non-English text: the text normalizer is English-tuned and
will mangle numbers and dates in other languages.

## Expression controls

> **Beta.** Emotion control steers delivery rather than guaranteeing it, and the effect
> varies by voice and by sentence.

```python
m.generate("[joyful] We won the grant <laugh> I can (((hardly))) believe it!",
           voice="Kiki", preset="expressive")
```

A leading `[emotion]` tag, inline `<event>` tags and `(((emphasis)))` spans reach the
model as markup rather than being spoken, and switch on its expression conditioning.

**Emotions** — one leading tag sets the emotion for the whole line:

`[angry]` `[contemplative]` `[excited]` `[joyful]` `[mundane]`
`[nervous]` `[sad]` `[stern]` `[surprised]` `[tender]`

**Vocal events** — inline, anywhere in the line:

`<gasp>` `<giggle>` `<growl>` `<gulp>` `<laugh>`
`<pause>` `<scoff>` `<sigh>` `<sob>` `<um>`

**Emphasis** — triple parentheses stress a word or short phrase:

```python
m.generate("I told you (((never))) to open that door.", voice="Victor")
```

Only these twenty tags are recognised. They are the most common of the many in the
training data, so a rarer one such as `[reverent]` is spoken as ordinary text rather
than treated as markup — as is anything else bracketed, like `section [3]` or `x < 5`.

## Weight variants

The language model ships in three packings of the same weights. `weights=` picks one;
`model.available_weights` lists them.

| `weights=` | On disk | |
|---|---|---|
| `"packed"` *(default)* | 954 MB | 1.58-bit ternary body, bf16 embedding. **Lossless** |
| `"emb4"` | 469 MB | Same body in TL2, plus a 4-bit embedding. **Lossy** |
| `"full"` | 3469 MB | Plain bf16 |

```python
m = KittenTTS("KittenML/kitten-tts-2", weights="emb4")
```

Only the variant you ask for is downloaded.

`emb4` halves the download, and the saving is almost entirely the token embedding — 324M
parameters that `packed` has to leave at bf16 because they are not ternary. Its transformer
body is still bit-exact: all 313 non-embedding tensors reproduce `full` exactly. The
embedding is not, at L2 relative error 0.118 against the bf16 export, and it is coded at
4.21 bits per weight across three frequency tiers. That is the one lossy thing here, which
is why `packed` stays the default.

## Decoders

Audio is decoded in two stages, and the first can be swapped for a smaller distilled
student with weights packed to 4 or 8 bits:

```python
m = KittenTTS("KittenML/kitten-tts-2", decoder="student_w4")
```

| Decoder | Flow on disk | |
|---|---|---|
| `default` | 459 MB | Best quality |
| `student_w4` | 39 MB | Distilled single-step student, weights packed to 4 bits |

These trade fidelity for footprint, not for speed: quantisation shrinks storage and
memory bandwidth, not arithmetic.

## What is in here

```
lm/          the speech language model, plus its spk_proj speaker head
speaker/     the speaker-embedding model used when cloning
voices/      reference clips, transcripts, and precomputed embeddings
decoders/    the optional 4-bit decoder
cpp/         GGUF weights for the llama.cpp fork, see "Running on CPU"
config.json  token layout, decode presets, voice and decoder indexes
```

The weights are 947 MiB: 910 MiB for the language model and 37 MiB for the decoder.
A load pulls those rather than the whole repository, and only the decoder you ask for.

The language model's linear weights are ternary — within every 128-wide group each
value is exactly one of `{-scale, 0, +scale}` — so bf16 spends 16 bits to say one of
three things. `lm/model-ternary.safetensors` packs them five trits to a byte, 1.6 bits
per weight, with each group keeping its scale at full precision:

| | |
|---|---|
| `lm/model.safetensors` | 3.47 GB, bf16 throughout |
| `lm/model-ternary.safetensors` | **0.95 GB**, the same weights, 3.6x smaller |

The packing is exact rather than approximate, so the two produce bit-identical audio.
`config.json` points `lm_packed` at the smaller file and that is what gets downloaded;
the full file stays for anything loading this with plain `transformers`.

## Running on CPU

KittenTTS 2 runs on CPU out of the box — `device` is auto-detected — but the fastest way
is [kitten-tts-2-cpp](https://github.com/KittenML/kitten-tts-2-cpp), our llama.cpp fork.
The `cpp/` directory here holds what it needs: the GGUF language model and its decoders.

## Requirements

Python 3.10 or later, and PyTorch.

## License

These weights are released under the [Stellon Labs Community License](LICENSE.md). Research,
non-commercial and limited commercial use are free of charge; the commercial grant ends once you
or your affiliates pass USD $1,000,000 in annual revenue or in total cumulative funding, at which

product built on them carries attribution requirements — see Section IV(a).

Two things in here are covered by their own terms instead: `speaker/`, the pyannote
speaker-embedding model, under [MIT](speaker/LICENSE), and the `kittenml` Python package that
loads this repository, under Apache 2.0.

# Crele Nimbus v1

**A real-time audio decision model.** Ask yes/no questions about live audio in plain English,
and get an answer every 40 ms, plus events when an answer starts and stops. It also knows who
is speaking: the user, or someone else.

Stream audio in at any chunk size; each answer arrives about a tenth of a second after the
moment it describes. Give it a few seconds of the user's voice, and two built-in signals follow
the user and everyone else, live (see [The user's voice](#the-users-voice)).

Built for voice agents: barge-in, end of turn, background sounds, another voice in the room.

**Website:** [crele.co/models/nimbus](https://crele.co/models/nimbus) · **Code:** [github.com/Crele-AI/nimbus](https://github.com/Crele-AI/nimbus)

## The user's voice

Most voice activity detectors answer one question: is anyone speaking? Nimbus answers two,
because a voice agent needs to know whose voice it is:

| Signal | Answers |
|---|---|
| `user` | Is the user speaking? The voice you enrolled |
| `other` | Is someone else speaking? Any other voice: another person in the room, or a voice from a TV or a loudspeaker |

Both are always on, answered every 40 ms beside your own questions, with events when they
start and stop.

**What it makes possible:**

- **Barge-in from the user only.** Stop talking when the user interrupts, not when someone in
  the background says something.
- **The user's end of turn**, even while other people are still talking.
- **Talking over each other.** Both signals can be yes at once, so you can see when someone
  speaks over the user, or the user over them.
- **Someone joins.** Notice another person or a TV voice, and adapt.

**Enrollment** takes a few seconds of the user speaking, recorded live or from a file (the
playground records five). A speaker-embedding model compares the voices in the stream with
that one.

```python
session.enroll(user_voice_16k)     # float32, mono, 16 kHz, a few seconds of speech

for update in session.push(pcm_16k):
    for event in update.events:
        if event.question == "user" and event.kind == "started":
            ...                    # the user started talking: stop the agent's speech
```

Without an enrollment, the model has no reference: `user` answers `cant_tell`, and `other`
cannot tell the user apart from anyone else. Enroll before relying on either signal.

Shown live on a microphone: the user alone, another voice near and far, turn taking, and
overlapping speech.

The enrolled voice becomes a voiceprint, which is personal data in many places: get the user's
consent, and store it as you would any personal data.

## What you can ask

Any yes/no question about what can be heard right now, in your own words:

- "Is music playing?"
- "Is someone typing on a keyboard?"
- "Is someone whistling?"
- "Is a siren wailing?"

Every answer is `yes`, `no` or `cant_tell`, with its probability. The two voice signals,
`user` and `other`, are always on beside them.

## Quick start

<!-- Provisional: the package's names are settled with the GitHub repository. -->

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/Crele-AI/nimbus
```

```python
from crele_nimbus import Nimbus

model = Nimbus.from_pretrained("crele/nimbus-v1")
session = model.session()
session.ask("music", "Is music playing?")
session.ask("whistle", "Is someone whistling?", threshold=0.5)
session.enroll(voice_16k)          # optional: a few seconds of the user's voice (see above)

for update in session.push(pcm_16k):   # float32, mono, 16 kHz, any chunk length
    for event in update.events:
        print(event.question, event.kind, event.start_s)
```

To try it in a browser with your microphone or an audio file:

```bash
python -m crele_nimbus.playground
```

The first run downloads about 1.5 GB: this model and the text encoder it uses.

## Tuning

Each question has four settings. The defaults suit most questions; change them per question.

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---:|---|
| `threshold` | 0.70 | An event starts when the probability rises above this |
| `start_secs` | 0.12 | ... and stays up this long |
| `stop_threshold` | 0.35 | The event stops when the probability falls below this |
| `stop_secs` | 0.30 | ... and stays down this long |

- A sound is missed: lower `threshold` for that question, for example to 0.5.
- A question fires too often: raise `threshold`.
- An event does not stop: the probability is resting above `stop_threshold`; raise it.
- Speech turns split at short pauses: raise `stop_secs`, for example to 1 s.

## Speed

- About 0.7 seconds of compute per second of audio (real-time factor 0.7) on an Apple M4 Pro
  laptop CPU, one stream, with 8 or with 32 questions.
- Asking more questions costs almost nothing: going from 8 to 32 questions adds about 1 ms per
  80 ms step. The audio is processed once per stream; every question reads from it.
- An answer arrives 80 to 120 ms of audio after the moment it describes, plus compute.

## How well it works

Measured on 500 real AudioSet clips with the default settings:

- **Says yes about 0.2 s after a sound starts**: a median of 0.24 s over the sounds it caught.
  For speech, 0.21 s, with 97% of 181 speech onsets caught.
- **Ask in your own words**: questions worded in ways it never trained on scored 0.892 against
  0.911 for its own wording (mean AUROC over 40 sounds, the same clips).
- **Quiet in a silent room**: the highest resting answer across twelve sound questions was 0.03.
- **Tells the user's voice from other voices**: shown live on a microphone with the user alone,
  another voice near and far, turn taking, and overlapping speech (see
  [The user's voice](#the-users-voice)).

## Limits

- English questions only.
- One user voice per session. Without a voice clip, the two voice signals have no reference.
- Audio is 16 kHz mono. Each answer is about the last few seconds of audio.
- Some sounds are recognised better than others; tune `threshold` for the ones that matter
  to you, and test on your own audio.

## How it is built

- A streaming audio encoder distilled from Dasheng-Base.
- A speaker-embedding model, CAM++ from 3D-Speaker, for the two voice signals.
- Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, unchanged, which reads each question once.
- A small decision head that answers every question from the shared audio.

About 97M parameters run on the audio. The text encoder (0.6B) runs once per question.

Trained with AudioSet and AudioSet-Strong, the AudioSet ontology, LibriSpeech, MUSAN and
FSD50K (CC0 and CC BY clips). The models and datasets, with their licences, are listed in
`NOTICE`.

## Files

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `listener.safetensors` | the streaming audio encoder |
| `head.safetensors` | the decision head |
| `speaker.safetensors` | the speaker-embedding model |
| `config.json` | the settings the model runs with |
| `LICENSE`, `NOTICE` | the licence and the attributions |

## Licence

Apache-2.0. See `LICENSE` and `NOTICE`.

```bibtex
  title  = {Crele Nimbus v1: a real-time audio decision model},
  author = {Crele},
  year   = {2026},
  url    = {https://huggingface.co/crele/nimbus-v1}
}
```

# Irodori Small MF for Core AI

Generate Japanese speech on an Apple device, with an optional reference voice. This FP32 conversion works with the [Core AI sample app and Swift runtime](https://github.com/oka-yuji/coreai-samples).

For developers exploring local speech generation on Apple silicon with macOS 27 or a physical iPhone with iOS 27. It is an experimental conversion with known waveform-fidelity differences. It does not support iOS 26, the simulator, or streaming speech. Building the sample requires Xcode 27 and Rust/Cargo.

## Quick start

In the iPhone sample app, open **Models → Irodori → Speech demo**, select **Reference voice (FP32)** and download the model. You can generate a voice from text alone, or supply your own recording or an audio file you have permission to use. See the [iPhone guide](https://github.com/oka-yuji/coreai-samples/blob/main/docs/irodori/iphone.md).

For a Swift project using `SpeechRuntime`, download the assets with the [Hugging Face CLI](https://huggingface.co/docs/huggingface_hub/guides/cli):

```sh
hf download okayuji/irodori-v4.1-small-mf-coreai-fp32 --local-dir ./Irodori
```

Build the sample repository's native input library with `Tools/Irodori/build-inputs.sh`, then use the runtime API:

```swift
import Foundation
import SpeechRuntime

let runtime = IrodoriRuntime()
_ = try await runtime.open(URL(filePath: "./Irodori"))
let audio = try await runtime.generate(text: "こんにちは。これは音声合成のテストです。", seed: 1708)
try audio.wav.write(to: URL(filePath: "./speech.wav"), options: .withoutOverwriting)
await runtime.release()
```

The folder is verified and copied into runtime-managed storage before use. Keep space for model files and specialization caches. Use a new output filename if `speech.wav` already exists. Reference input uses `SpeechReferenceAudio` from `SpeechCore` and `generate(text:seed:reference:)`; the app handles recording and audio-file conversion.

## Recorded output

Input text: `こんにちは。これは音声合成のテストです。`

<audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/okayuji/irodori-v4.1-small-mf-coreai-fp32/resolve/main/samples/text-only.wav"></audio>

The included example is **5.48 seconds**, generated without a reference recording using seed `1708`. It is a synthetic voice, not a microphone recording. This example's generation interval was not recorded separately.

A separate synthetic-reference check used approximately **3.86 seconds** of reference audio and produced **4.00 seconds** of output. Reference → no-reference → same-reference generation returned identical repeated-reference WAVs. The release assets also produced byte-identical reference and no-reference WAVs to the earlier assets. These correctness checks ran on M4 Max, macOS 27.0 (26A428), Xcode 27.0 (27A266a), FP32, one request at a time. See the [release verification record](https://github.com/oka-yuji/coreai-samples/blob/main/docs/irodori/release-asset-validation.json).

An earlier run with the original v2 assets reported **1.276 seconds** for its reference generation on the same M4 Max/macOS/Xcode configuration, one request, seed `1708`. This is the runtime's generation interval, excluding folder verification, text normalization/tokenization and audio-file decoding/resampling. The historical log did not record cache state. This is a single recorded observation, not a device performance promise or a speed comparison with this release. The [verification record](https://github.com/oka-yuji/coreai-samples/blob/main/docs/irodori/release-asset-validation.json) includes this historical observation; the [runtime guide](https://github.com/oka-yuji/coreai-samples/blob/main/docs/irodori/reference-runtime.md) describes earlier failures.

## Input and files

- Japanese text, up to **255 body tokens**; four MeanFlow steps.
- Optional reference: **48 kHz mono Float32**, **0.5–30 seconds**, finite and non-silent. The app converts supported audio files to this format and rejects an overlong recording instead of silently truncating it.
- Output: **48 kHz mono Float32 WAV**. Empty caption, no tail trimming, no added watermark.
- Model payload: **20 files, 3,835,379,527 bytes (3.84 GB)**. Documentation, licenses and the audio example are additional. File size is not the working-memory requirement.

The six components are the text encoder, reference-audio encoder, speaker encoder, conditioned duration predictor, conditioned DiT, and codec decoder. `irodori.json` identifies `irodori-coreai-v2` and the asset inventory digest. The sample app pins the tokenizer and all component files. The legacy v1 text-only inventory remains separate.

## Verification

The four added reference components passed individual PyTorch/Core AI FP32 checks on the Mac. The preliminary Python end-to-end check passed the exploratory NRMSE **0.001** threshold with a **0.5-second** reference (**0.00072797**) and missed it with an approximately **8.26-second** reference (**0.00171340**, cosine **0.99999853**, matching **114 frames**). That miss remains unresolved; it is not a listening score.

The native runtime disables frequent-reshape specialization for the audio encoder, speaker encoder and conditioned duration. DiT keeps its existing policy. The iOS codec decoder also disables it to avoid a dynamic-allocation assertion. Repeated-reference equality and the **0.5/30-second** input boundaries passed on the Mac. All-EFR execution previously returned different durations after switching voice modes; that failure is retained in the runtime record.

Source debug locations were removed with the Core AI authoring API. Generic MLIR including all constants and resources, with only locations omitted, matched before stripping, after stripping and after reading the saved assets in separate processes. This preserves the existing model computations; it does not resolve the original-PyTorch fidelity difference.

The earlier reference diagnostic completed three generations and WAV saving on **iPhone 17 Pro / iOS 27.0.1**. That diagnostic did not capture a microphone or assess listening quality. Its [device report](https://github.com/oka-yuji/coreai-samples/blob/main/docs/irodori/reference-input-device.json) identifies the assets and conditions used.

## Limitations and troubleshooting

- Original-PyTorch waveform parity is not established for the native reference path. Speaker similarity and naturalness have not been scored.
- First specialization can take longer and needs additional storage and memory. The model-file size does not establish iPhone working-memory or endurance requirements.
- Captions, arbitrary-length references, multiple reference recordings and streaming output are not implemented by this bundle.
- `This model does not support a reference voice. Choose the reference-voice model.` means a legacy bundle was selected. Do not rename a v1 folder or edit its manifest to make it look like v2.
- A hash mismatch requires the matching release files and runtime version. The original PyTorch checkpoint cannot be opened directly by this runtime.
- A generated voice can coincidentally resemble a real person. This does not grant permission to present synthetic speech as that person's actual speech.

Irodori, the Japanese codec fine-tune, ModernBERT-Ja and its Sarashina2 tokenizer ancestry use MIT terms. The original DACVAE code and base weights retain Apache-2.0 terms. The corresponding license texts, copyright notices, source revisions and conversion changes are in [LICENSE](LICENSE) and [NOTICE](NOTICE); the upstream terms continue to apply to their components.

# PsarAI-Speech-GGUF

Fast Khmer / English / French speech synthesis for [audio.cpp](https://github.com/0xShug0/audio.cpp), in the Jarvis
voice or **a voice cloned from a reference clip**, mixed sentences (Khmer + English, Khmer + French) included.
Many times faster than real time on GPU (see Speed).

numbers → words → characters → speaker-conditioned T2U (Transformer, CTC over 1,000 mHuBERT-147 speech units,
+ **unit 4-gram** beam search) → durations and **pitch** → unit HiFi-GAN with speaker + pitch input, 24 kHz. The
speaker is a CAM++ embedding (192 values): the built-in Jarvis one, or computed from `voice_ref`.

## Voice cloning

Pass a few seconds of clean speech as `voice_ref` (server) and the reference voice sets the accent, rhythm,
melody and timbre:

```json
{"model": "psarai-speech", "input": "សួស្តី លោក។ Good evening, sir.", "voice_ref": "/path/to/reference.wav"}
```

It copies pitch and voice type (male / female, high / low); the speaker is recognisable but not identical yet
(similarity to the reference ~0.46 vs ~0.8 for two real clips of the same person). Use clean recordings: noise in
the reference is taken as part of the voice and makes the speech hard to understand.

**Numbers are read out** in the text's language (the voice itself cannot read digits): `2026`, `1 500,50 €`,
`$25.50`, `15%`, `14h30` / `10:30`, `1er` / `3rd`, `XXIe siècle`, `25°C`, `120 km/h`, `-4`, `2020-2025`, French
phone numbers, Khmer digits (`២៥`). The language is detected per sentence and script run, so mixed Khmer / English /
French text works; the `language` option (km, en, fr) forces one.

| Text | Spoken |
|---|---|
| `តម្លៃ 25 ដុល្លារ ក្នុងឆ្នាំ 2026។ ម៉ោង 14:30 សីតុណ្ហភាព 32°C។` | តម្លៃ ម្ភៃប្រាំ ដុល្លារ ក្នុងឆ្នាំ ពីរពាន់ម្ភៃប្រាំមួយ។ ម៉ោងដប់បួន សាមសិបនាទី សីតុណ្ហភាព សាមសិបពីរអង្សាសេ។ |
| `The price rose 15% to $1,234.50 in 2026.` | The price rose fifteen percent to one thousand two hundred and thirty-four point fifty dollars in twenty twenty-six. |
| `Il coûte 1 500,50 € en 2026, à 14h30 le 1er mai.` | Il coûte mille cinq cents virgule cinquante euros en deux mille vingt-six, à quatorze heures trente le premier mai. |

Number-heavy sentences transcribed back by ASR (chrF, higher is better): Khmer 20 → 80, English 28 → 71, French
21 → 71 with the conversion vs reading the digits.

Speech recognition is a separate repo: [PsarAI-Speech-ASR-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/nphearum/PsarAI-Speech-ASR-GGUF)
(Unsloth Studio shows one task per repo).

Family **`psarai_speech`**. It needs audio.cpp with the patch in [`audiocpp/mms_asr.patch`](audiocpp/mms_asr.patch)
(families `mms_asr`, `psarai_s2s`, `psarai_speech`; not in upstream audio.cpp).

## File

| File | Size | |
|---|---:|---|
| `psarai-speech-f32.gguf` | 0.36 GB | T2U with pitch predictor + vocoder (78M parameters, fp32), CAM++ speaker encoder (7M), Jarvis voice embedding, unit 4-gram tables |

## Quality

20 held-out clips per group, text → speech → ASR (content CER, lower is better) and CAM++ similarity of the speech
to the reference voice (higher is better). "Previous" is the October 30 version of this file (Jarvis only).

| Group | previous: CER | this, Jarvis voice: CER | this, cloned: CER | cloned: similarity (previous) | two real clips |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Jarvis texts | 6.8% | **4.7%** | 4.9% | 0.74 (0.73) | 0.74 |
| DDD Khmer speakers (held out) | 18.1% | **12.6%** | 13.7% | 0.48 (0.02) | 0.79 |
| designed voices (held out) | 12.5% | **10.4%** | 12.8% | 0.46 (0.12) | 0.83 |
| FLEURS Khmer | 22.0% | **18.0%** | 41.8% | 0.35 (0.14) | – |
| FLEURS English | 8.0% | **7.3%** | 39.2% | 0.35 (0.21) | – |
| FLEURS French | **5.0%** | 5.5% | 25.3% | 0.39 (0.22) | – |

Greedy units, no listen-back. FLEURS references are noisy real recordings (hence the cloned CER) and their speakers
are unknown, so the reference is the clip itself.

Against the Python reference package: identical speech on short sentences, also when cloning (correlation 1.0);
on long texts the unit 4-gram beam can take a different, equally good path (floating-point differences between
ggml and PyTorch). The number conversion is a C++ port, identical to the Python version on 27,000 test strings.

## Speed

RTX 3090, audio.cpp server (times include HTTP and WAV I/O), warm, median of 3, measured while another training
job kept the GPU at 100%:

| Text | Jarvis | cloned (CAM++ on the reference every request) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 3.6 s of speech | 0.086 s (42×) | 0.102 s (35×) |
| 6.8 s | 0.12 s (57×) | 0.15 s (43×) |
| 67 s (chunked) | 1.08 s (62×) | 1.06 s (58×) |

The previous version measured 110–135× on an idle GPU; this one adds a pitch predictor and speaker inputs.

## Use with audio.cpp

```bash
git apply audiocpp/mms_asr.patch          # upstream commit 50749561
cmake -S . -B build -DENGINE_ENABLE_CUDA=ON -DAUDIOCPP_MODELS="mms_asr;voxcpm2;psarai_s2s;psarai_speech" && cmake --build build -j
build/bin/audiocpp_cli --task tts --family psarai_speech --model psarai-speech-f32.gguf --backend cuda \
  --text "សួស្តី លោក។ Bonsoir, monsieur." --out hello.wav
```

Server: `{"id": "psarai-speech", "family": "psarai_speech", "path": "psarai-speech-f32.gguf", "task": "tts", "mode": "offline"}`,
then `POST /v1/audio/speech` (`{"model": "psarai-speech", "input": "..."}`) → 24 kHz WAV.

Request options: `pace` (default 1.07, >1 slower), `unit_lm` (default true), `numbers` (default true),
`language` (km / en / fr; default: detected), `text_chunk_size` (default 300 code points; longer texts are spoken
sentence by sentence with 0.2 s pauses), `voice_ref` (reference clip to clone; default: Jarvis).

## Limitations

- One synthetic voice that imitates a fictional character's voice; the rights to that voice belong to its owners.
- Cloning copies voice type, not identity; noisy references fail. Rare number formats (fractions, scores) may be
  read digit by digit or as ranges.
- The Python package's listen-back check (ASR hears the speech and retries) is not in the GGUF.
- Not in upstream audio.cpp: stock builds (and Unsloth's own prebuilt) cannot load `psarai_speech`.

## License

**CC-BY-NC-4.0** (non-commercial). Speech units from
[utter-project/mHuBERT-147](https://huggingface.co/utter-project/mHuBERT-147); speaker encoder CAM++
(FunASR / 3D-Speaker, weights from ResembleAI/chatterbox, MIT).

# OGG TTS **Expressive multilingual text-to-speech with block diffusion**
> **Preview release.** This is checkpoint 40k of a 400k-step pre-training run that is still in progress. The model > already speaks intelligibly in all 8 languages, while voice similarity, tag control and multi-speaker scenes keep > improving. Updated checkpoints will be published as new revisions of this repository; the 20k preview stays > available in the history. ## Overview OGG TTS is a 0.8B-parameter zero-shot text-to-speech model trained on about 8,000 hours of professionally acted speech in English, Polish, Spanish, German, Russian, French, Portuguese and Italian. It generates discrete tokens of the Fish Audio 44.1 kHz codec with **block diffusion**: - each block of 0.74 s is produced in parallel by iterative unmasking; - blocks follow one another left to right, so audio can be streamed as soon as the first block is ready. The backbone is initialised from OmniVoice (Qwen3-0.6B, masked discrete diffusion). A lightweight multi-token prediction (MTP) decoder then fills in the acoustic detail of the block, also by iterative unmasking. The name comes from the trolls of *The Witcher*. OGG is the first of three architectures (OGG, ROGG, POGG) that we compare in an upcoming technical report. ### Highlights - **Expressive by default.** The model is trained on audiobook productions with full voice casts and on AAA game dialogue, so it reads with natural, context-appropriate emotion. - **Optional inline tags.** 24 tags for emotion, delivery and vocal events, placed exactly where they should take effect. - **Zero-shot voice cloning.** From a few seconds of reference audio, or one of the built-in speaker identities without any prompt. - **Multi-speaker scenes.** A whole dialogue is generated in a single pass, with natural turn-taking and pauses. - **Streaming.** Finished blocks never change and can be played immediately. ## Emotion and expression tags Tags are optional. Without them the model infers the delivery from the text and its context. With them it follows the requested emotion or sound at the given position: ```text [frustrated] Not again… [sighing] Fine, I'll do it myself. [scared] [whispering] Someone is here… [shouting] Run! They're right behind us! ``` | Group | Tags | |---|---| | Emotion | `[angry]` `[frustrated]` `[excited]` `[tired]` `[playful]` `[sad]` `[scared]` `[shouting]` | | Delivery | `[whispering]` `[softly]` `[voice breaking]` `[singing]` `[pause]` `[slowly]` | | Vocal events | `[laughing]` `[sighing]` `[gasping]` `[panting]` `[coughing]` `[clears throat]` `[sniffling]` `[scoffing]` `[yawning]` `[humming]` | The labels come from an audio-language-model pass over **502,668 sentences**, i.e. the audio with its transcript, under a closed list of 24 tags. The model was instructed to tag only what is audible in the recording, never what the text alone suggests. 57,016 sentences (11 %) received at least one tag; the rest carry a checked transcript without tags, so the model also learns when *not* to add an effect. Tags are dropped from part of the training samples, which keeps them optional at inference time. | Tag | Examples | Tag | Examples | Tag | Examples | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | `[shouting]` | 19,407 | `[laughing]` | 2,621 | `[tired]` | 708 | | `[angry]` | 10,287 | `[scared]` | 1,847 | `[slowly]` | 419 | | `[frustrated]` | 5,565 | `[whispering]` | 1,502 | `[clears throat]` | 356 | | `[pause]` | 4,065 | `[playful]` | 1,380 | `[humming]` | 346 | | `[excited]` | 3,980 | `[gasping]` | 1,266 | `[coughing]` | 333 | | `[sighing]` | 3,738 | `[scoffing]` | 1,010 | `[panting]` | 248 | | | | `[sad]` | 894 | `[voice breaking]` | 144 | | | | `[softly]` | 887 | `[singing]` | 95 | Rare tags (`[singing]`, `[yawning]` 59, `[sniffling]` 46) have too few examples to be reliable. Tag control is still weak in early checkpoints and strengthens as pre-training continues. ## Model architecture | Component | Details | |---|---| | Backbone | OmniVoice / Qwen3-0.6B, 28 layers, d = 1024. Bidirectional attention within a block, block-causal across blocks; earlier blocks are seen with all 10 codebooks | | Acoustic decoder | MTP: 9 chained transformer layers, one per residual codebook, 164M parameters; each layer unmasks its codebook over the frames of a block (masked prediction), seeing the codes already decided | | Total parameters | ~0.81B (codec excluded) | | Audio codec | Fish Audio Drama 3 / S2 codec, 44.1 kHz, 21.5 frames/s, 1 semantic codebook (4096) + 9 residual codebooks (1024) | | Block size | 16 frames (0.74 s) | | Decoding | 6 confidence-ordered unmasking iterations per block with classifier-free guidance, then the MTP unmasks the 9 residual codebooks of the block in 4 rounds each; KV cache, ~0.17 real-time factor on one GPU | | Length | predicted by the model (end-of-speech token) | ## Usage Requires the [code from GitHub](https://github.com/FashionFlora/ogg-tts), the OmniVoice weights (`k2-fsa/OmniVoice`) and the Fish Audio codec (`codec.pth` from `fishaudio/drama-3`). ```bash git clone https://github.com/FashionFlora/ogg-tts && cd ogg-tts git clone https://github.com/fishaudio/fish-speech ogg_tts/fish-speech export OMNIVOICE_PATH=$(huggingface-cli download k2-fsa/OmniVoice) export FISH_CODEC_PATH=$(huggingface-cli download fishaudio/drama-3 codec.pth) ``` ```python import sys, torch sys.path.insert(0, "ogg_tts") from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download from safetensors.torch import load_file import omnifish as of, infer_omnifish as inf, fish_codec as fc model, tok = of.OmniFish.from_omnivoice() model.load_state_dict(load_file(hf_hub_download("FashionFlora/ogg-tts", "model.safetensors"))) model, codec = model.cuda().eval(), fc.load_codec("cuda") codes = inf.generate(model, tok, None, "", "[sighing] Hello! I am OGG, a text to speech model.", "en", steps=6, cfg=2.0) audio = fc.decode(codec, codes[None].cuda())[0].float().cpu().numpy() # 44.1 kHz ``` For voice cloning, pass the reference audio's codes (`fc.encode`) together with its transcript. For a dialogue, give one prompt per voice and mark the turns: ```python ptext = "<|quad_start|>S1<|quad_end|>transcript of prompt 1 <|quad_start|>S2<|quad_end|>transcript of prompt 2" scene = of.dialogue_text([("S1", "Did you hear that?"), ("S2", "Hear what?"), ("S1", "Someone is following us.")]) codes = inf.generate(model, tok, torch.cat([codes1, codes2], 1), ptext, scene, "en", speaker="dialogue") ``` ## Training data About **8.2k hours** of studio-quality speech from 584 audiobooks and games, 16,628 speakers: | | | |---|---| | Sentences | 6.1M | | Speech (sentence audio, without inter-sentence pauses) | ~7,200 h | | Codec frames (21.5 Hz) | 559M | | Codec tokens (10 codebooks) | **5.6B** | | Text tokens (Qwen3 tokenizer) | ~112M | | Language | Hours | Speakers (≥ 10 min) | |---|---|---| | English | ~2,610 | 986 | | Polish | ~1,300 | 359 | | Spanish | ~820 | 473 | | German | ~750 | 217 | | Russian | ~645 | 237 | | French | ~500 | 192 | | Portuguese | ~300 | 165 | | Italian | ~290 | 90 | **Sources:** - multi-cast audiobook productions (full voice casts and sound design, with music and effects removed); - single-narrator audiobooks; - the voiced dialogue of four AAA games. **Processing:** - vocal source separation; - sentence segmentation; - diarisation and speaker grouping; - a sentence-level speaker-verification pass over 1.85M lines; - transcript verification and spoken-form normalisation with an audio-language model. ## Training | | | |---|---| | Hardware | 1× NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB) | | Schedule | 400k steps, 16k tokens per step, AdamW, cosine decay, bf16 | | Throughput | ~190 hours of audio per training hour | | Audio seen | ~22k hours over the full run (~1.7B frames, ~17B target codec tokens) | | Sequence tokens | 6.6B (400k steps × 16k tokens: text, prompt and target frames) | ### Compute and cost | Stage | GPU time | Cost | |---|---|---| | Codec tokenisation (8.2k h) | 28 h | $95 | | Sentence-level speaker verification | 12 h | $40 | | Experiments: pilot, 5 discarded runs, batch-size tests | 20 h | $70 | | Pre-training, 400k steps (estimated) | 113 h | $380 | | **Total** | **~173 h** | **~$580** | GPU cost is computed at the AWS on-demand rate for `g7e.2xlarge` (~$3.36/h). | Annotation | Volume | Cost | |---|---|---| | Transcript verification and audio tags (audio-language model) | 502,668 sentences, ~324M tokens (253M input, 71M output) | ~$455 | At list prices (Gemini Flash, $0.75 / $3.75 per 1M input / output tokens). Data preparation on CPU (source separation, segmentation, diarisation) is not included. The figure includes the prompt iterations: three versions of the annotation prompt, and the emotion tags were re-done once after `[frustrated]` was added to the list. **Experiments.** Before the final run we trained five shorter runs that were stopped and discarded: - a first model without block diffusion (16.6k steps), which showed that the OmniVoice backbone adapts to the Fish Audio codec; - a block-diffusion run of 38k steps, the reference for the final recipe; - three short runs (2k–4k steps) that tested the data pipeline: speaker-change-centred dialogue scenes, continuous single-speaker windows and the unmasking MTP decoder. Together with the pilot and the batch-size tests they took about 20 GPU hours (~$70), so roughly an eighth of the GPU budget went into experiments that did not end up in the release. **Final cost of the released model (complete 400k-step run, projected from the measured training speed):** | | GPU time | Cost | |---|---|---| | Final model: tokenisation, speaker verification, pre-training 400k steps | ~153 h | ~$515 | | Annotation (transcripts and tags) | | ~$455 | | **Final model total** | | **~$970** | | Experiments (not part of the release) | 20 h | ~$70 | | **Project total** | **~173 h** | **~$1,040** | All of it on a single GPU, in about a week of wall-clock time. ## Evaluation Evaluation is in progress and will be reported with the final checkpoint. - **Benchmarks:** Seed-TTS (EN) and CV3 (PL, DE, FR, ES, IT, RU, PT). - **Metrics:** WER/CER, speaker similarity, UTMOS, tag compliance, real-time factor. ## Limitations - Preview checkpoint: speaker similarity is not yet final, and the model may still mispronounce rare names. - Italian and Portuguese have the least training data. - Rare tags are not reliable yet. - Multi-speaker scenes with several very short turns can still drop a line in this checkpoint. ## License and responsible use - **Fish Audio codec.** The model generates Fish Audio codec tokens and needs the Fish Audio codec to produce audio. Use is subject to the [Fish Audio Community License](https://huggingface.co/FashionFlora/ogg-tts/blob/main/LICENSE-FISH-AUDIO.md) (see `NOTICE`). - **Real voices.** Do not use OGG TTS to imitate the voice of a real person without their consent, to impersonate, deceive, defraud or harass anyone, or to create sexual content involving minors. - **Training data.** It contains copyrighted recordings, and the weights are released for research. ## Citation ```bibtex @misc{oggtts2026, title = {OGG TTS: Expressive Multilingual Text-to-Speech with Block Diffusion}, author = {FashionFlora}, year = {2026}, url = {https://huggingface.co/FashionFlora/ogg-tts} } ```

# VoxCPM2 - BFloat16 (full precision)

MLX port of [openbmb/VoxCPM2](https://huggingface.co/openbmb/VoxCPM2) — a 2B-parameter multilingual TTS model with 48kHz studio-quality output, voice cloning, and voice design.

Full precision BFloat16 weights. Best quality, largest size.

## Features
- **30 languages** — including English, Chinese, Indonesian, Japanese, Korean, and more
- **48kHz output** — studio-quality audio
- **Voice Design** — create voices from text descriptions (no reference audio needed)
- **Voice Cloning** — clone any voice from a short audio reference
- **4 generation modes** — zero-shot, continuation, reference cloning, combined

## Usage

```bash
pip install mlx-audio

# Zero-shot
python -m mlx_audio.tts.generate --model mlx-community/VoxCPM2-bf16 --text "Hello world" --verbose

# Voice design
python -m mlx_audio.tts.generate --model mlx-community/VoxCPM2-bf16 \
  --text "Hello world" \
  --instruct "A young woman, gentle and sweet voice"

# Voice cloning
python -m mlx_audio.tts.generate --model mlx-community/VoxCPM2-bf16 \
  --text "Hello world" \
  --ref_audio speaker.wav --ref_text "reference text"
```

### Python API

```python
from mlx_audio.tts import load_model

model = load_model("mlx-community/VoxCPM2-bf16")

# Generate
for result in model.generate(
    text="Hello, this is VoxCPM2 on Apple Silicon.",
    inference_timesteps=7,
    cfg_value=2.0,
):
    print(f"Duration: {result.audio_duration}")
```

## Performance (Apple Silicon)

| Variant | Size | RTF (7 timesteps) |
|---------|------|--------------------|
| bf16 | 4.96 GB | 0.48x |
| **8-bit** | **3.23 GB** | **0.85x** |
| **4-bit** | **2.30 GB** | **0.90x** |

*RTF = Real-Time Factor (>1.0 = faster than realtime)*

# Audio8-TTS-Kurdish-Sorani

A **Central Kurdish (Sorani)** fine-tune of Audio8 TTS, a 0.6B-parameter DualAR text-to-speech model with zero-shot voice cloning. Neither Central Kurdish nor Persian is among the base model's supported languages. Training started from the Persian fine-tune [ArminRahimi/Audio8-TTS-Persian](https://huggingface.co/ArminRahimi/Audio8-TTS-Persian), whose script Sorani largely shares. <!-- If you trained from the original Audio8 (INIT_MODEL = "base"), change this sentence and base_model above to Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6b. -->

Training code, Colab notebook and documentation: **https://github.com/ard9/Audio8-Persian-TTS**

> **Non-commercial use only.** The training data, [central-kurdish-tts4all](https://huggingface.co/datasets/aranemini/central-kurdish-tts4all), is licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, so this model is released under **CC BY-NC 4.0**: free for research, education and non-commercial demos; not for paid products or services.

## 🔊 Samples

| Text | Audio |
|---|---|
| سڵاو، ئەمڕۆ کەشوهەوا زۆر خۆشە و دەمەوێت کەمێک لە پارک پیاسە بکەم. | [ft_s01.wav](samples/ft_s01.wav) |
| دوێنێ لەگەڵ هاوڕێکانم چووین بۆ سینەما، فیلمەکە بەڕاستی زۆر جوان بوو! | [ft_s03.wav](samples/ft_s03.wav) |
| Voice clone (reference from another speaker of the dataset) | [clone_s01.wav](samples/clone_s01.wav) |

## Usage

The model uses Audio8's custom Transformers code (`trust_remote_code=True`). Normalize the text with the same Sorani rules as in training (`normalize_ckb` in the GitHub repo: Arabic letter variants unified, numbers spelled out in Kurdish).

```python
# pip install "transformers>=4.57,<5" soundfile
# git clone https://github.com/ard9/Audio8-Persian-TTS  (for fa_tools.normalize_ckb)
import sys, torch, soundfile as sf
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoProcessor
sys.path.insert(0, "Audio8-Persian-TTS/src")
from fa_tools import normalize_ckb

model_id = "ArminRahimi/Audio8-TTS-Kurdish-Sorani"
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True, dtype=dtype).eval().to(device)

text = normalize_ckb("سڵاو! چۆنی؟")
inputs = processor(text=[text], return_tensors="pt")
# Voice cloning: add reference_audio=["ref.wav"], reference_text=[normalize_ckb("exact transcript")]
inputs = {k: v.to(device) for k, v in inputs.items()}
with torch.inference_mode():
    out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024, temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95, top_k=50,
                         do_sample=True, return_dict_in_generate=True)
    wav, lengths = model.decode_audio(out.codes)
sf.write("output.wav", wav[0, : int(lengths[0])].float().cpu().numpy(), model.config.codec_sample_rate)
```

Or from the command line: `python scripts/synthesize.py --model ArminRahimi/Audio8-TTS-Kurdish-Sorani --lang ckb --text "سڵاو" --output out.wav`.

## Training details

| | |
|---|---|
| Starting model | Audio8-TTS-Persian (itself fine-tuned from Audio8-TTS-Preview-0.6B, repo commit `07e40f5`) |
| Data | central-kurdish-tts4all: ≈ 35 h of read Central Kurdish, 3 speakers (male and female audiobook narrators, male studio voice), 24 kHz, clips of 1–20 s |
| Default voice | The speaker with the most audio is trained without a reference clip; the other speakers always with a same-speaker reference, which teaches voice cloning |
| Text normalization | Sorani rules: Arabic yeh/kaf → Kurdish forms, ھ → ه, heh + ZWNJ → ە, diacritics and ZWNJ removed, numbers spelled out in Kurdish |
| Trainable parameters | Both DualAR branches (slow + fast AR), all 601M parameters |
| Optimizer | 8-bit AdamW, lr 3e-5, cosine schedule, 3% warmup, grad-norm clip 1.0 |
| Steps / epochs | TODO |
| Hardware | TODO GPU on Google Colab |
| Exported weights | bf16 |

## Limitations

- **Three speakers, read speech.** Voice variety and prosody are limited; conversational speech and unseen voices are weaker.
- **Possible Persian accent** when starting from the Persian model, especially in early checkpoints.
- **Spelling follows the dataset**: the model learns pronunciation from how the transcripts are written; non-standard spellings and Latin-script words may be mispronounced.
- The base model is a Preview checkpoint without Kurdish or Persian pre-training.

This model can imitate voices. Clone a voice only with the speaker's explicit consent and disclose synthetic audio. Do not use it for impersonation, fraud or misinformation, or to imitate the dataset's speakers.

# Qwen3-TTS 1.7B Base on the Apple Neural Engine

This is a Core ML build of [Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base), the
**voice-cloning** model. It clones a voice from a few seconds of reference audio plus its transcript, and runs it on
the Neural Engine of a Mac. It needs no GPU, MLX or ONNX Runtime.

It's built for [Gloam Voice Studio](https://gloam.fm) for Mac by [Tiny Trash Labs](https://tinytrashlabs.com).
The Swift runtime that loads it is the open-source `QwenANE` target in
[TinyTrashLabs/gloam-voice-studio](https://github.com/TinyTrashLabs/gloam-voice-studio)
(see `Sources/QwenANE/README.md`).

## What's in it

| Path | What it is | Runs on |
|---|---|---|
| `coreml/talker0.mlmodelc` … `coreml/talker3.mlmodelc` | The talker transformer, as four stateful chunks (KV cache inside Core ML) | Neural Engine |
| `coreml/cp_ane.mlmodelc` | The code predictor (15 sub-codes per frame) | Neural Engine |
| `coreml/upF.mlmodelc`, `coreml/upMall.mlmodelc` | The vocoder upsampler | Neural Engine |
| `coreml/QwenSpeechEncoder.mlmodelc` | The reference audio → codec codes encoder, for on-device voice prep | Neural Engine |
| `coreml/QwenSpeakerEncoder.mlmodelc` | The reference audio → speaker embedding encoder, for on-device voice prep | Neural Engine |
| `host/` | Tokenizer, config, the text embedding and projection, the codec embeddings | CPU (Accelerate) |
| `vochead/` | The vocoder head (pre-transformer and quantizer) | CPU (Accelerate) |

Requires **macOS 15** or later (stateful Core ML models). The set is about 2.7 GB. It is too large for 8 GB iPhones; on an
iPhone use [the 0.6B build](https://huggingface.co/tinytrashlabs/Qwen3-TTS-0.6B-Base-ANE).

## What's different from the other Core ML ports

- **Base, not CustomVoice.** It clones any voice rather than offering preset speakers, and both encoders are
  included so a new voice can be prepared on the device.
- **One read is one performance.** `QwenTalkSession` / `renderBreak` split long text and carry each part's text and
  codec frames into the next part's prompt. They draw the whole read from one sampler stream and redraw a derailed
  take, so pace and tone don't reset at every split.
- **Exact sampler.** It reproduces numpy's `default_rng(seed)`, so a seeded render is reproducible and comparable to the
  Python reference.
- **Streaming.** Decoded audio arrives in 0.96 s chunks, and the first chunk can be shortened for lower latency.

## Speed

It makes better clones than the 0.6B build and is slower: in our tests about real time on an M5 Mac, so it streams
only just ahead of playback. Your numbers will vary by Mac and thermal state.

## Use

```swift
import QwenANE

let engine = try QwenANEEngine(modelsDirectory: modelsURL)      // the downloaded folder
let voice  = try QwenVoicePrep.prepare(referenceWAV: wavData, transcript: "exactly what the clip says",
                                       modelsDirectory: modelsURL)
let session = QwenTalkSession(engine: engine, voice: voice, language: "en", seedText: text)
let read = try session.renderBreak(text, onPart: { part in print(part.logLine) })
// read.samples: mono Float at read.sampleRate (24 kHz)
```

## License and attribution

The original model is © the Qwen team (Alibaba Cloud) and licensed under the
[Apache License 2.0](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base). This repository is a
**modified redistribution** under the same license (see `LICENSE`). Changes from the original:

- converted to Core ML (fp16, stateful talker split into four chunks)
- the vocoder split between Core ML (upsampler) and CPU arrays (head)
- the text embedding stored quantized

The model weights were not fine-tuned.

Only clone your own voice, or a voice you have permission to use.

# Pocket TTS for sherpa-onnx in six languages

Kyutai's [Pocket TTS](https://github.com/kyutai-labs/pocket-tts) as ONNX files that the unmodified
[sherpa-onnx](https://github.com/k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx) 2.0 Pocket TTS engine loads, one folder per
language. Used by [HaexVault](https://github.com/haex-space/haex-vault) for local speech output.

| Folder | Language   | Source bundle                                     |
| ------ | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `de`   | German     | KevinAHM `onnx/german`                            |
| `en`   | English    | k2-fsa `sherpa-onnx-pocket-tts-int8-2026-01-26`   |
| `es`   | Spanish    | KevinAHM `onnx/spanish`                           |
| `fr`   | French     | KevinAHM `onnx/french_24l` (only a 24-layer model exists) |
| `it`   | Italian    | KevinAHM `onnx/italian`                           |
| `pt`   | Portuguese | KevinAHM `onnx/portuguese`                        |

Every folder holds the files of a sherpa-onnx `OfflineTtsPocketModelConfig`: `lm_flow.int8.onnx`,
`lm_main.int8.onnx`, `encoder.onnx`, `decoder.int8.onnx`, `text_conditioner.onnx`, `vocab.json`,
`token_scores.json`. Pocket TTS has no built-in voices: pass a short reference recording as
`GenerationConfig.reference_audio`.

## Attribution and licence

- Model weights: Kyutai, [kyutai/pocket-tts](https://huggingface.co/kyutai/pocket-tts), CC BY 4.0.
- ONNX export: KevinAHM, [KevinAHM/pocket-tts-onnx](https://huggingface.co/KevinAHM/pocket-tts-onnx)
  at revision `58a6d00cf13d239b6748cb0769f35c580a8f606c`, CC BY 4.0. The English folder is the
  k2-fsa sherpa-onnx release `sherpa-onnx-pocket-tts-int8-2026-01-26` of the same export.
- `vocab.json` and `token_scores.json` were converted from each bundle's `tokenizer.model` with
  sherpa-onnx [`scripts/pocket-tts/convert_tokenizer.py`](https://github.com/k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx/tree/master/scripts/pocket-tts).

This repository is distributed under CC BY 4.0 as well (`LICENSE`).

## Changes

Only `encoder.onnx` of `de`, `es`, `fr`, `it` and `pt` differs from the source.

The multilingual bundles expect a learned start embedding (`bos_before_voice.npy`,
`insert_bos_before_voice: true` in `bundle.json`) in front of the voice embedding. sherpa-onnx 2.0.1
does not insert it, and without it these models find no end of the sentence and produce noise.
[`tools/add_bos_before_voice.py`](tools/add_bos_before_voice.py) appends the embedding as a
`Concat` in front of the output of `mimi_encoder_int8.onnx`, so the encoder output already starts
with it:

    python add_bos_before_voice.py --encoder mimi_encoder_int8.onnx \
      --bos bos_before_voice.npy --output encoder.onnx

The script needs `onnx` and `numpy` and gives byte-identical files. It is proposed upstream in
[k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx#4148](https://github.com/k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx/pull/4148). The other files are renamed only:

| `lm_main.int8.onnx`     | `flow_lm_main_int8.onnx`     |
